#3855. Ubisoft lay off 166 more staff, this time at their Montreal and Quebec City studios, while mumbling about "current production priorities and business needs"

"Our production needs are changing," publishers claim

Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada. Both studios affected, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, had a hand in last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows, with Montreal especially being a major and long-tenured development hub for the company.

Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

"Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft said in a statement handed to both sites. "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

Ubisoft Montreal are currently working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, reportedly a witchy tale set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire, which switched creative directors earlier this ear and is one of the games Ubi are keen to get out of the door. What Quebec have been up to since Shadows shipped is less clear. They're a much smaller than Montreal and were founded in 2005.

Ubisoft have been carrying out mass cuts across their studios worldwide all the way through this year. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx. Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona. Long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm. Ubisoft's Paris HQ. Three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz. All have been subjected to some form of cuts or closure.

Meanwhile. changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Solidarity to all of the Ubisoft workers who've been affected by these layoffs in Montreal and Quebec.

#3854. Ubisoft says Assassin's Creed Jade is still alive as it merges two of its Creative Houses

Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.

Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet said mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.

"Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said. "Today, we can say that console and PC remain our core focus for our biggest franchises."

He added: "The focus is really to make sure that we come with strong growth on console and PC, and notably PC, which is a more dynamic platform than ever."

Ubisoft last confirmed its China-set mobile game was still in the works in March, when it was mentioned in the publisher’s Assassin's Creed: Into 2026 blog. Assassin's Creed now sits within Vantage Studios, Ubisoft's joint venture with Tencent, which launched last year.

Ubisoft's results also confirmed some more changes to the way the company is run, with the publisher saying its new operating model is "now fully in place". Creative Houses 3 and 5 have been combined under the leadership of Julien Bares "to leverage synergies between Live experiences across platforms".

All leadership roles across the Creative Houses are now filled, too. An external general manager has been appointed for Creative House 4 and is set to join in January 2027, though Ubisoft hasn't yet confirmed who. That follows September's appointment of 2K and Amazon Games veteran Christoph Hartmann to lead Creative House 2, home to The Division, Ghost Recon, and Splinter Cell, which was renamed Massive Entertainment at the same time.

Outside the Creative Houses, Motherbrain, the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI experiment Teammates, is now a subsidiary in its own right. It's working on "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds". A separate unit has also been set up to look after brands that don't belong to any of the Creative Houses.

Ubisoft says the new structure is already paying off, pointing to the commercial success of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and renewed momentum for Rainbow Six Siege, which it says ranked among the top 10 games across Xbox and PlayStation for monthly active users over the half.

That said, the publisher nonetheless posted a net loss of €254.5 million for the first half of the year, with net bookings down 16.5 percent to €644.7 million.

The news comes just hours after Ubisoft confirmed 166 job cuts at its Montréal and Québec City studios, the latest in a year of layoffs. They're part of the "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" that Ubisoft announced in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

On the weekend, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

US President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he'd given Nvidia "assurance" that ousted and now reinstated CEO Jensen Huang did not represent a national security threat despite an affair with a woman who was reportedly in contact with China's top spy agency.

Trump provided that assurance without any formal investigation into Huang's dealings.

On whether Huang had been investigated, US Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a press conference this week, "I don't want to talk about investigation. What does that mean, had Huang been investigated? For what? I don't understand the question."

Blanche also said that he did not know about any export control investigation related to Nvidia, even though potential violations of export control law are the central concern of the scandal.

"A critical national security threat in the Nvidia situation is that Jensen Huang shipped extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer said on Tuesday.

According to sources speaking to Reuters, Trump's assurance to the Nvidia board was based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, the latter of which is the company associated with Alice Huang (no relation), the woman with whom Huang admitted to having an affair. (The CEO also reportedly had affairs with Nvidia employees.)

In his return address to Nvidia staff, Huang said (via Marisa Kabas) that the company's board opted to bring him back of their own accord, not because of pressure from the Trump administration. That statement is contradicted by Trump himself, who told CNBC that he "convinced" the Nvidia board to bring Huang back.

Huang is scheduled to testify before the US Senate next Thursday, December 3.

#3852. Blizzard wants to "get rid" of best-in-slot items in World of Warcraft: Forever by introducing situationally strong gear

"BIS is not a good thing for a game that's supposed to be about role-playing."

With World of Warcraft: Forever's first raids set to release in early December, developers of the game have spoken about endgame itemisation and their desire to disrupt the "best-in-slot" (BIS) mindset that's been at the core of WoW's progression for years.

This information stems from the latest episode of the official World of Warcraft: Forever podcast. In it, senior game designer Aidan Moon revealed his philosophy around the game's itemisation, which he played - and plays - a major role in designing.

"I essentially want to get rid of BIS," Moon said. "I think BIS is not a good thing for a video game that's supposed to be about role-playing. That's why I've introduced the creature subtype system, where things are more effective against murlocs [for example]. We've introduced the biome system too, and in the raid it's different."

He gave an example from upcoming raid Barrow Deeps, which will be split into different biomes that offer opportunities for such creature subtype gear to be put to use. "If you go to the left wing that's snowy; if you go to the right wing, that's haunted; if you go down below, that's cavernous. ... I think your BIS should be different for every single boss if you're making a theoretical BIS list."

Moon acknowledged that the system is open for players to interact with to the extent they're comfortable with. Some players might bring optimised gear for certain bosses, while others might not, opting instead for generally good gear to perform well regardless of the fight.

It's an excitingly different approach that goes against the established norms of WoW's endgame raiding. In other versions in World of Warcraft, gear progression is more linear: people go into raids with an idea of what gear drops are best for their character, and intentionally hunt these pieces to replace the set they're wearing. It's a vertical sense of progression. Will theoretically having multiple sets of equipment, for multiple situations, change this?

Best-in-slot gear is an especially pertinent topic in WoW Forever at the moment, given the most dedicated players are reaching max level, or nearing it, and are hunting for items in preparation for the upcoming raid. I'm currently ticking off equipment from a best-in-slot list for a Balance Druid. Whether this player behavior will change when the changes are implemented remains to be seen. Perhaps the approach will expand, with players continuing to hunt down generally accepted 'good' items while also seeking side pieces that provide situational bonuses along the way.

The Blizzard discussion on raid itemisation went beyond standard power items. Chase items, those with especially low drop rates, were also talked about by Moon, noting that Barrow Deeps continues several such items that he hopes will keep players returning to it for years to come.

The items Moon is likely referring to here probably relate to mounts, pets, situational gear, and perhaps campfire bonuses.

For example, I obtained an upgraded campfire earlier in the game that allows a greater campfire to be built that allows more buff items to be placed around it.This has essentially locked me in as a campfire slave for the upcoming raid tier, and valuable to a raid composition.

World of Warcraft: Forever has proven extremely popular since its early November release. The game broke franchise records for Blizzard on launch, and has more weekly players than WoW has seen in 15 years. Judging from early impressions of World of Warcraft: Forever, the game has real merit.

#3851. Ignore that other game about crime that's out and burgle some ugly farmhouses in Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" with a 2000s Cartoon Network vibe

Is there something going on today? A lot of talk about committing crimes and the like, I just can't quite put my finger on why… Ah well, couldn't be important or interesting. What is interesting, however, is Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" that has launched on this inauspicious day about stealing stuff from "hideous farmhouses in the middle of nowhere."

With the sarcastic intro out the way, I will address the elephant in the room: Vovly's Adventure: Reslimed is out today too. Fine, fine, yes I know GTA 6 is the game everyone's talking about, but Forward Instinct, the devs behind Keepsake County, seem well aware of that in their launch day post for the game: "Folks, thanks for your incredible patience. Keepsake County is finally OUT! And yes, it is deeply ironic that it wound up being today, of all days, that we got the green light to finally release, but here we are."

Keepsake Country was supposed to release earlier this month, but seemingly got caught up in the backlog Valve are faced with that's undoubtedly been caused by genAI games. In any case, the burgle-em-up does look quite delightful. I'm not sure if I can quite put my finger on exactly why I get this feeling, but it calls to mind a more complex version of the kind of game you'd find on Cartoon Network's website back in the day (which is a high point of praise, I'd like to be clear).

Each house in Keepsake Country is procedurally generated, meaning you never quite know what to expect when you enter. There's lockpicking, resident tie upping, and of course stealing to be done, but it doesn't just stop at the house. Parking your car, for instance, is an important thing to consider; do you want it hidden so you're less likely to be discovered, or right at the front door so you can make a speedy escape? Not to mention you have to deal with the fuzz showing up at some point if you aren't quick enough!

Gear and the like can be improved between runs, meaning you can lockpick faster or delay the cops, it all seems quite systemically thoughtful. Very much some immersive sim vibes from this one, just on a much smaller scale. And most certainly worth considering picking up on a release day like today! If you're interested in doing so, you can pick it up on Steam right here.

You've got great timing, because no matter what you want to make (be it cool miniatures for D&D, props for cosplay, or something else entirely), this is the best time of year to shop. Black Friday 3D printer deals regularly provide record low prices on all sorts of machines, but especially newcomer-friendly ones that can introduce you to the hobby with as little fuss as possible.

Actually, there's almost too much choice. I've been using and writing about these machines at GamesRadar+ for years now, so have put that knowledge to good use in finding you the best offers on 3D printers for beginners. The two I've chosen were selected based on extensive hands-on experience, and they just so happen to have been slashed in cost for 2026's Black Friday 3D printer deals.

Before we get started, it's important to narrow down what you're hoping to make. Don't worry, I've got a quick breakdown for you in case it's helpful. Hoping to make terrain, props, tokens, or generally useful stuff like dividers for the best board games? Filament printers are the way to go, because they produce the strongest results. Looking for incredibly high-detail miniatures to use in D&D and Warhammer, or more precise cosplay gear? Resin printers are what you want. I've included my entry-level picks for both of these below, and they've been chosen because I think they do the best job of introducing you to the fundamentals. Indeed, they're what I use at home right now...

No matter whether you're new to 3D printing or have experience with the hobby, I think this may be my favorite filament machine. Besides being incredibly easy to use (something I praised in my Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo review), it comes with multi-color print functionality so that you can create more advanced projects without having to manually swap out material. Plus, it being so enclosed keeps things tidy and much quieter too. To cap things off, I'm pretty sure that's a record low price.UK: £398 £329 at Elegoo (with code)

Even though they're smaller spools (most normal ones are 1KG, whereas these are 250g each), this multi-color pack is a great way to kick off your hobby and provide the widest range of shades as cheaply as possible. It's never been cheaper than it is now for this year's Black Friday 3D printer deals.UK: Currently unavailable, here's a good alternative at Amazon

If you want a fuss-free, foolproof way of printing resin miniatures that isn't going to make you want to tear your hair out, this is the perfect choice. As noted in my Anycubic Photon P1 review, it's able to overcome any problem you throw at it due to a user-friendly interface, a heated vat to avoid failures if you're printing in a colder environment, incredibly high print resolutions, and a new 'Wave Release Technology' for a better overall print. When you throw in good positioning accuracy and stability to avoid failures, it's a great choice.UK: £649 £399 at Anycubic

If you're buying a resin 3D printer, you'll need one of these - a wash and cure machine. That's because models aren't ready once they're made in the printer; they've got to be rinsed off with either IPA or water (depending on the resin you've used) and then cured using UV lamps. It's not a particularly drawn-out process, but it is important. If you're getting Anycubic's machine, I'd go for its accompanying Wash and Cure system for ease.UK: £113 £79 at Anycubic

Want the easiest entry-point to resin 3D printing with the least fuss? I'd recommend water-washable resin, because you don't then need to worry about grabbing smelly IPA as well. With this material, you can just use normal water in your wash and cure machine which is much, much easier to then dispose of.UK: £21.80 £13.59 at Amazon

Still not sure which kind of 3D printer for beginners you should get? Personally speaking, I'd recommend filament machines to start with. These are a no-mess option that help you learn the ropes fast, but without all the cleanup required with goopy, toxic resin. Modern filament printers can also produce surprisingly detailed models as well, so you can kinda make whatever you like so long as you're happy to lose some resolution on particularly small miniatures. D&D models made with a filament machine aren't gonna look anywhere close to as good as those produced by a resin 3D printer, of course, but that's probably OK if you're just starting out.

No matter what you go for, I hope you have an amazing time with your first projects! Enjoy it - this is an amazing hobby, and even now after many years making ridiculous prints, it still feels a little bit like magic to me.

#3847. Space station horror-FPS Derelikt is a lively retro throwback to Alien: Resurrection, though it's better at shooting than scaring

I'm a reasonable man. I don't expect every PS1-styled, cosmic horror, nakedly Alien: Resurrection-homaging retro FPS to suffocate me under a blanket of misery. Some of the lighter moments in Derelikt, which released last week, even land: I was grinning my cheeks off as I gorged on the Eldtrich knowledge sealed within an alien obelisk, while repeatedly hanging up on the aghast scientist who kept videocalling me to stop.

Still, Derelikt is fortunate that it's a good shooter, as it often gets muddled on whether it wants to be a horror game as well. It certainly threatens the spooks, trapping you in an oppressively dingy asteroid rig in the orbit of Saturn - the scariest of the ringed gas giants! - and warping most of the other staff into vaguely echinodemic monsterpeople. Also, opening the inventory reveals it to be made of rectangles, a classic symptom of a video game character about to get mangled in the nerves and face.

But nah, shotgun go boom boom. It turns out Derelikt's derelict dwellers are both perfectly susceptible to mundane lead, and sparing users of ambush tactics at most; several even stand around with their backs turned, as if waiting for you to surprise them with a lethal pipe swing. And, even on Medium difficulty, the opening spell of fight-or-run scarcity quickly gives way to an abundance of ammo and health pickups that can easily fill the pocket grid to bursting. I don't claim to have been playing perfectly, but I'm about halfway through and the only way I see myself running low on bullets is if I start using them to punch the complete works of Thomas Campion into a wall.

It's indecisive tonally, as well. The dialogue, and there are a fair few survivors to chat with, seems interested in emulating the gravitas-starved, "Woah man" style of New Millennium action game scripts. Which I can sort of see the logic behind, given the visuals and sound design also, and arguably much more painstakingly, mimic that era. But the downside remains that it ends up with a gravitas-starved, "Woah man" style, just with an extra dash of sideways-winking awareness. Again, it only sometimes works, and it's never scary or eerie. But then there are also more earnest attempts to spin uneasiness, with pages of deranged scribbles left behind by the dwindling crew, and at least a couple of genre-classic wall daubings, which tend to leave me wishing developers Visuwyg had just picked a lane.

Again, though, underneath all the smartarsing is a quality little shooter. The retro presentation does little to soften the heavy, industrial kick of its gunfire, and although many of the meatier freaks are more absorbent than they look, their pained thrashing really helps sell the impact of every individual shot. I also don't really mind the lack of Dead Spacey surprise attacks, as the station's narrow confines tend to force you into tenser, close-range encounters in an organic way anyhow.

More impressive still is how Derelikt manages to fabricate a cold, apprehensive atmosphere befitting its fallen space base, in direct defiance of its own quasi-comedic script. This is mainly thanks to the clanging, low-lit station itself, which teases you with just enough flashes of comfort – a stretch of marble floor here, a messy rec room there – to make your quick return to its steel guts feel all the more unpleasant. Some credit must also go to the puzzling, the cardkey hunts and code searches of which initially had me fearful of the more obstinate, opaque, classic horror style preferred by fellow backwards-looker Silver Pines. Instead, it's more like a compacted Deus Ex, hinting at the need to peek at people's computers and scour the environments for the needed codes. Which makes for generally smoother progress, yes, but also gets you more involved and present inside Derelikt's infested walls.

Midway-through impressions, then: it's a little silly, and perhaps a little confused, but Derelikt finds its focus whenever something needs making dead. I shall continue blasting xenos and burning my eyes out with magic rocks until – no, madam, please hold – further notice.

Exoprimal was intriguing, but it never caught fire with players.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Exoprimal is a throwback to weird, experimental early 2000s Capcom," we wrote of the team-based hero shooter ahead of its launch back in 2023. While ostensibly about battling dinosaurs, "you first go through an interdimensional time portal controlled by a rogue AI, and then you compete in a Hunger Games-style contest against alternate universe versions of yourself for the AI's amusement. That's where the dinosaur killing comes in."

Despite that intriguing premise, the end result was not particularly memorable: Perfectly fine, and with some fantastic ideas, but "more like an early access phase than a finished game," we wrote in our 69% review. And it didn't catch on: A year later, Capcom announced the end of new updates for the game, although the game remained fully playable.

But now that's changing too. Capcom announced today that Exoprimal services will be terminated on September 29, 2027, at which point the game will become unplayable. "We cannot thank you enough for the love and support you have shown over the years," Capcom wrote, "and we sincerely apologize for the gravity of this announcement."

The sale of seasonal "survival passes," which have been rotating through Exoprimal's four seasons since the end of updates in 2024, has been halted, while the game itself along with all DLC and "other products"—there's quite a lot of it—will be removed from sale on March 30, 2027. After that, the game will tick on—and Capcom hopes you will continue to enjoy it—until the end of the road in September.

It sucks to see games fail, especially when they have the potential to grow into something good, and it's even worse when they don't just tank but become completely unplayable because of their reliance on external servers that no longer exist. This is one of the primary drivers behind efforts like Stop Killing Games: Wherever possible, the end of a game's service should not signal the end of the game.

It's a principle I broadly support, but in the case of Exoprimal it's fair to say that not too many people will be impacted by the shutdown: SteamDB indicates that the peak concurrent player count over the past 24 hours was just 23. Exoprimal is also available on consoles so there are more players in total than just that, but how many more? I don't know, but I'd guess not too many.

#3845. GTA 6 day-one sales are enormous, estimates suggest, making previous $2 billion opening weekend predictions seem conservative

Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have sold nearly 25 million copies in one day, generating approximately $2.5bn in sales revenue - a staggering result that's beyond even what even observers were predicting.

The estimates come from data-tracking company Sensor Tower (spotted by VGC), which has been watching GTA 6 pre-orders closely for weeks, updating estimates daily based on (unspecified) data that it collects.

Should the results be accurate, it'll dramatically eclipse GTA 6's $1bn in three days result. It'll also put GTA 6 on track to reach the eye-watering $3.25bn to $5.2bn week-one sales estimates for GTA 6.

So far, Rockstar has said nothing in relation to GTA 6's sales since the game was released around the world yesterday. Parent company Take-Two has said the game's pre-orders were tracking "well above expectations, and GTA 6 broke pre-order records on both the PlayStation Store and the Xbox Store, though, so all signs point to a record-breaking release. The question is "by how much?".

Reaction to GTA 6 has been glittering. Chris awarded GTA 6 five golden stars in Eurogamer's review, calling it "a game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale". "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that."

#3844. Valve are pausing Steam Machine 2TB orders over "supply constraints," though the 512GB model is free of its waitlist

Valve giveth, and Valve taketh away in their latest Steam Machine availability update. The dinky SteamOS PC continues to have a terrible time with AI industry-inflicted hardware parts shortages, which at least for its flagship 2TB model, have become such a problem that Valve are suspending new orders until further notice. While Valve's post says that they "have wrapped up sending purchase invites out to all remaining 2TB reservation holders" – meaning if you'd previously reserved one, you'll still get your chance to buy – "supply restraints" have put the kibosh on any new orders for now.

It's not all bad news, though. The cheaper 512GB Steam Machine has achieved "add-to-cart status", which is Valve's slightly odd way of saying you can snap one up without having to join a reservation waitlist. Just like in the Before Times! The post does add that 512GB stock is still limited, so that might sell out too if they can't source enough parts to build new ones, though this is still the first time that the refreshed Steam Machine has been waitlist-free since launching in June.

One could, with the aid of a Torx screwdriver and a conveniently illustrated guide, work around the 2TB model's lack of existence by nabbing a readily available 512GB Machine and replacing its stock SSD with a chunkier aftermarket drive. A not-terrible, budget two-gigster can be had from £240, which when added to the 512GB Machine's £879 outlay, actually works out a little less than buying a 2TB Machine as is. SteamOS is free to download and install, and swapping out the Steam Machine's SSD is considerably easier than the plasticky brain surgery of Steam Deck drive replacement.

Of course, ideally none of that would be necessary, and we could all fill our living rooms with sub-£700 Steam Machines that had never been choked by the greedy hands of industrial-scale RAM hoarders. But that's not the world we live in. Indeed, Valve end the post by rather chillingly suggesting that their hardware prices may rise yet again.

"We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units," they say, "but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels; as a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained."

"We anticipate having more information to share come January."

#3843. Review: Zero Parades: Director's Cut (PS5) - A Riveting Spy Thriller That Still Lacks Disco Elysium's Bite

Version Reviewed: PS5 (Standard) / European

I’m on sub-level three of a long-abandoned rocket silo, reading heavily redacted files by flashlight. Most of the screen is black, save for a little pang of light from my torch, and my heart beats rapidly as I comb through reams of text on the right of the screen.

It’s not flashy nor is it a massive spectacle, and it’s taken me hours to get to this point. However, it may be one of the most engrossing gaming moments I’ve had on PS5 this year.

This game is Zero Parades: Director’s Cut, the spiritual successor to ZA/UM’s enormously praised Disco Elysium, which has finally made its way to PS5 after launching on PC earlier in 2026.

It’s a text-and-dice-based RPG, where Operant (read: spy) Cascade has returned to the town of Portofiro five years after an assignment went horribly wrong. This is her chance at redemption.

However, upon arriving in Portofiro, she finds her double comatose in their safe house, and with no clue as to what her assignment actually is, Cascade must take to the streets.

What you’ll find there is a massive, sprawling collection of mysteries that weave and connect in myriad ways. A girl’s plea to help find her missing dad may link to a poetry magazine that could be a front. A cosmonaut figure in the bustling bazaar was my first thread that eventually led me to read through documents underground in the dark 20 hours later.

Admittedly, there are times that pacing is to its detriment. The opening hours are especially slow, as you get a lay of the land. However, like any good mystery thriller, I'm of the opinion you have to put in the time before you can reap those mysterious rewards. It's not going to be for everyone — which should be obvious with the whole text-and-dice-based RPG descriptor — however, if it is your thing, then your patience will pay off.

Zero Parades is a familiar game for anyone that played Disco Elysium, but it does have its own unique identity. There’s a lot of crossover, from the style of narration to the stacked-against-you odds of its dice-driven actions. However, where Disco is a more internal reflection of our initially nameless detective, Zero Parades sprinkles some of that in with a deal more narrative mystery, and I love that about it.

Cascade is basically a f*ck up, haunted by the elusive errors of her past, so while you may have the skill somewhere inside of you to be a good spy, it’s but a fleeting thing. It’s entirely down to how you level up Cascade, across the faculties of action, relation, and intelligence to define the kind of spy you are.

Kicking off my investigation, I pile a ton of points into intelligence skill, particularly Technoflex, the study of all things tech. Sometimes this skill is subtly useful, like being able to fix the fax machine in the photo printing store where my safe house is located. Other times, it proves its worth in big ways, like being able to bypass the security lock of a secret prison, because I am aware of a system flaw in that precise model.

However, there is real flexibility to Zero Parades’ exploration and progression. For example, that secret prison has multiple ways in, and you may be able to talk yourself in via the front door if you have the right skills levelled up.

By the time you figure out your assignment, the narrative has laid the foundation for many different approaches, and each can take you on its own weird road through the streets of Portofiro, and your success down those roads is dependent on how you build up your character.

And let me be clear: you can simply fail in Zero Parades – it’s sort of the crux of the whole experience. Whether it’s a botched escape from a mysterious man, or completely messing up an attempt to construct a homemade gun, Zero Parades is brilliant at making it feel like the odds are stacked against you.

That is emphasised all the more with the stress system. Across fatigue, anxiety, and delirium (which relate to your action, relation, and intelligence upgrades), certain actions will build up pressure in any three of these gauges. As it ascends, Cascade will be hit with nerfs of varying severity, and if the scale maxes out, it will refresh and deduct a skill point for its related skill group.

There are ways to juggle this, of course. Smoking cigarettes, eating sweets, or certain drinks can lower specific gauges whilst increasing others, and sleeping is possible to reduce all gauges but is time-locked. You are then able to exert yourself to increase the chances of hitting the required dice numbers, but this comes at the cost of increasing the scale of its related gauge.

The whole experience becomes a balancing act while trying to figure out which gauge may still require space to carry out certain actions. Maybe you decide not to engage in some activity for fear of needing it in something more important. Or maybe you spend it all wanting to cover everything, and then suffer the consequences when you really need it in a pivotal story moment.

This whole system means I am vehemently aware of Cascade’s physical and mental state at pretty much all times across the story. It also means that no part of the game’s content is trivial, as it all ties into one and other, not just narratively but mechanically. What I do now directly impacts what I can do later.

By the time the credits rolled, my ending felt especially my own. My own failures, successes, and regrets. And it massively encourages me to go for another try, to hopefully unlock new avenues, level up in different areas, and maybe even finish successfully (I messed up badly).

As you can tell, I am a big fan of this game, but it doesn’t get everything right. For one, the writing is great, as you would hope for, but it lacks the same razor edge that Disco Elysium has in spades. Voice acting is generally brilliant, but at times it feels like a game doing its best Disco impression, with a yearning to be as edgy as possible.

I did come to like Cascade’s voice performance a lot more as I spent more time with it, but it undeniably lacks the same punch as Lenvel Brown’s dulcet tones as The Narrator in Disco Elysium.

Then we come to the PS5’s performance. I played this on both PS5 and PS5 Pro, and the performance is surprisingly bad. For 90% of the game, as you talk to various characters, it’s obviously not an issue – you’re mainly just looking at still screens as text moves down the right side. However, when you’re running around the town of Portofiro, the frame rate consistently tanks.

It’s a shame because the art style is quite gorgeous, as it somehow mixes a painterly art style with a simultaneously dull aesthetic. Like in the story, Portofiro is a town of stalled potential, left to rot over its beauty. DualSense haptics are also surprisingly great, albeit subtle. It really makes you feel like you're flicking through redacted documents with nuanced ripples at your fingertips.

Zero Parades: Director’s Cut is a dense and highly detailed text-based RPG, that moves at a painstakingly slow pace. However, it’s part of the magic of this story. It lacks the same authenticity as Disco Elysium, but manages to hold its own with a riveting mystery that very naturally unfolds.

It’s riveting when a small detail links back to the previously abandoned thread, and you feel like a spy yourself as you try to piece it all together. It lets you relish in the world and revel in the chaos, and as the credits rolled, I just wanted to jump back in and try it all over again.

Review copy provided by ZA/UMHow we review productsScoring Policy

Swearing an oath of loyalty to PlayStation with the arrival of the PS4, our resident video-maker and Irn-Bru loving Scot prides himself as an expert in modern-day Sony. However, eight playthroughs of The Last Of Us later, and no Platinum to show for it, will forever be his greatest shame.

Nah. Too many good games out there to reward the suits that hollowed out ZA/UM. Honestly wouldn’t even pirate it, leaves a completely bad taste.

@nessisonett you prompted me to remind myself of the whole torrid affair. It remains awful what the studio did, so I'm of like mind I feel (this is a great review though!)

I wonder when we'll start to see any of the 3/4 games in development by the various off-shoots from staff that left or were pushed out, they all sounded exciting!

Clicky Islands came out on the heels of a certain game from Rockstar, too

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

May I remind you, GTA 6 wasn't the only game to come out in the last two weeks. Clicky Islands, a fun throwback island builder published by Palworld company Pocketpair, arrived earlier in the month, and according to the publisher's estimates, it's doing very well indeed.

On Twitter, John 'Bucky' Buckley, the head of publishing and communications at Pocketpair, takes a second to highlight just how successful the game's been. "Clicky Islands launched ten days ago, and it's smashed every target!" he writes. "Really proud to be supporting this game and the two Polish wizards who cooked it up!"

It is a delightful little gem that merges citybuilding and idle game ideas. Essentially, you land on a remote island, and start making it more habitable for your people, but how you do that is distinctly streamlined – you mostly just click around and let things be built, gradually accruing more resources.

Clicky Islands launched 10 days ago, and it's smashed every target! Really proud to be supporting this game and the two Polish wizards who cooked it up! 🇵🇱 A devilishly addictive incremental game that blends clicker elements with city building! A real gem! https://t.co/oOu58lP7IrNovember 26, 2026

As Pocketpair's monster-collecting survival adventure continues to grow, more opportunities for games like this can and will emerge, and it's good to see that money and energy being put to good use. If Clicky Islands is anything to go by, I'd keep an eye on what else the publisher may have in store.

Meanwhile, Buckley's been teasing that we'll hear more about Palfarm and the coveted Palworld 1.1 soon. No rest for the wicked – unless Rockstar's about to put something out, that is.

Cyberleek, the GTA 6 leaker or leakers who shared a bunch of alleged gameplay earlier this year, are now claiming to have released a nearly complete in-development build of the crimsim's Xbox version. Continuing their established grift, the leaker or leakers are threatening to release the main executable file they've withheld unless people pump up the value of their cryptocurrency.

"It is done," a statement posted on Cyberleek’s website claimed. "CL holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto VI, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one - the main executable - held on a countdown. Honest terms, as always: it is an Xbox build this time, not a PC build. CL does not care. This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps. CL told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons."

So, more anime villain chatter from Cyberleek, who claim the executable file is on a timer and will be released immediately if their crypto coin reaches a $15 million market cap. It looks like the build is yet to be confirmed as genuine.

If any build leak were to result in GTA 6 being emulated on PC in rapid fashion, that would threaten to undercut an official port. Rockstar have yet to confirm that such a port is on the way and when it'll drop, but an October report from GamesBeat claimed the first three months of 2027 as the window in which Rockstar plan to deliver the game to PC. Former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij recently told our Edwin he reckons that concerns about unofficial ports based on the console version of GTA 6, likely made with generative AI, might lead Rockstar not to leave too big a gap before bringing the crimsim to PC officially.

Any alleged playable unofficial port of GTA 6 made with help from genAI and chucked online could, of course, just be a great big pile of malware.

Rockstar, who previously called the initial barrage of leaks laid claim to by Cyberleek "heartbreaking", as well as parent company Take-Two, looked to have begun a hunt for the identity of the leakers back in August.

#3840. Total War: Warhammer 40,000 breaks the game into star system mini-campaigns, each with their own stories and objectives

"We want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy."

There is perhaps nothing so brutal in a Total War game than getting an army full of elite units wiped out, and it appears that pain remains a factor in the upcoming Total War conversion of : Warhammer 40,000. Creative Assembly also has some nifty ideas around breaking the game into mini-campaigns for each star system you visit.

In an hour-long deep-dive livestream of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, developer Creative Assembly demonstrated the game in action, focusing initially on how armies navigate from planet to planet. Each star system apparently acts as a "contained campaign" you can hop between in the game.

The star system the stream focused on is Praevoss, a mid-sized collection of planets: three of which you can land on and fight on, while the others are smaller and unable to support your tactical warfare shenanigans. Once you're finished with a star system, you move on, carrying over units and unlocked skills.

"First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," Creative Assembly explained on the livestream. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start, [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do."

One of the objectives highlighted in the livestream was an Ork Scourge, which required the player - controlling Space Marines - to hold the planet while eradicating the Ork presence.

As you can imagine, much of the stream was dedicated to the fleet of spaceships at your disposal - fleet movement and management, and the abilities they provide to your armies such as orbital bombardments. There was also detail on how ships transport troops, as well as the upgrades you can build to further enhance their power.

On the topic of transporting troops, the developers focused on the small number of expensive but powerful Space Marines they controlled. These Space Marine armies come with a potentially "devastating" cost if you mess up and lose your armies during one of the star system campaigns.

"Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the developers explained. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that."

Total War: Warhammer 40,000 is set to release some time in 2027, though no specific date has been established as of writing. Much has been seen at this point on its gameplay, galactic or otherwise. As we near the end of the year, fans are clamouring for official word on when they can take to the stars.

#3839. Amid a year of layoffs, Ubisoft yank the cover off Motherbrain, their new studio "focused on AI for gameplay innovation"

Something something "proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators" something something

Ubisoft have revealed their Motherbrain. It's far less cool than it sounds. Rather than being a giant floating slab of thinky meat that can do telepathy, Motherbrain is a studio dedicated to doing development stuff with generative AI. As you might expect, it consists of the folks who worked on Ubisoft's "first playable generative AI experience".

Motherbrain's reveal as "a dedicated subsidiary focused on AI for gameplay innovation" came via Ubisoft's latest earnings report, where the company trumpeted that their "new operating model" is "now fully in place". The model is the reorganising into creative houses responsible for different game series that Ubisoft announced at the start of this year, with leaders for all of the houses now arranged.

"We have also established Motherbrain, the team behind our first playable generative AI experience Teammates, as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators and open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences," CEO Yves Guillemot said.

You'll never guess what his next few lines were. "We remain on track with our cost reduction program, reflecting our commitment to a focused and disciplined organization as we are preparing for a significantly stronger content cycle," the exec said. "In parallel, we have made progress on our refinancing plan with the objective of securing competitive terms and putting in place an efficient medium-term plan over the coming months."

That'd be the wave of layoffs and closures Ubisoft have been rolling out all through this year, most recently getting rid of 166 staff at Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, both of which worked on Assassin's Creed Shadows. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx, Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona, long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm, Ubisoft's Paris HQ and three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz are all on the list of bits of the company affected in some way by the cuts.

Changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Ah well, at least there's seemingly money there to support the developing of those proprietary technologies infused with genAI brainiacery.

If you've played over a hundred hours of Vampire Survivors you've probably forgotten how slow its early progression feels. It certainly seemed that way based on the reaction to Warhammer Survivors from Vampire Survivors veterans, who complained about its grindiness compared to their beloved bullet heaven originator, despite the arc of both games being quite similar. Developers Auroch Digital made Warhammer Survivors in partnership with Vampire Survivors creator Poncle, so of course the two games have a lot in common.

Other complaints were more valid. The Beasts of Nurgle did have too many hit points, and their ability to regenerate only exacerbated that. The treasure chest-opening animation did take a bit too long. And some of the weapons were undertuned. Fortunately, those issues and more have been addressed in hotfix v2.18. Here are the highlights:

The change to XP is an interesting one. It's a standard part of the genre's formula to have random XP drops—killing some enemies gives you nothing, while others drop XP gems and tempt you to rush into a mob to grab them. Making every enemy drop at least a low-value XP gem will speed up leveling a bit, but hopefully when you see green or red gems you'll still want to risk a mob of orks to yoink.

Auroch Digital recently revealed a roadmap of upcoming additions to Warhammer Survivors, with the first big update in December promising more characters, weapons, and weapon evolutions. January's updates will add more quality-of-life and balance improvements, as well as cross-save, with another update in the first quarter of 2027 bringing another round of characters, weapons, and weapon evolutions.

The final item on the roadmap is a tease that simply says, "ERROR… Details classified." It's probably not the addition of a whole extra universe to its current Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar settings, but I'd be stoked to see them add the other popular world of Warhammer. By which I mean Blood Bowl, of course.

#3837. UK Prime Minister won't be playing GTA 6, government says, while hailing Rockstar Games a "British success story"

Grand Theft Auto 6's seismic launch has registered on a governmental level. A spokesperson for UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has hailed the game as a "British success story", but confirmed Burnham himself won't be playing it. His diary is apparently "very full".

"Rockstar Games is a British success story made in Edinburgh," a Downing Street spokesperson told The Independent - referencing the series' Scottish origins and ongoing development at Rockstar North - "and many fans are already saying GTA has been worth the wait." When asked if Burnham will be making time for GTA 6, the spokesperson responded: "His diary is very full. He won't be playing it."

Downing Street went on to address the issue of teenagers potentially skipping school to play the game, emphasising that children "should be in classrooms" this week because "every day in school matters".

The leader of Labour's opposition, the Conservative party's Kemi Badendoch, recently expressed similar concerns. "I know people are worried about the game content," she wrote. "At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half-an-hour on it and then went out and did something else."

GTA 6's culture-shaking success was unlikely to pass without reference by the government, but the celebratory tone is a marked departure from Burnham's predecessor Kier Starmer calling Rockstar's firing of 34 staff last year "deeply concerning". We are awaiting a verdict in the resulting employment tribunal related to it.

This state recognition of GTA 6 is not without precedent. It wasn't long ago that French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on its award-winning and heart-winning success. That game sold 8 million copies in one year; GTA 6 is estimated to have sold 25 million copies in one day.

GTA 6 has been hailed as a generational release - an exorbitantly luxurious game that "pushes back the horizon of video games", Chris Tapsell wrote in Eurogamer's GTA 6 review.

#3836. Akira Kurabayashi, company director at Arika and developer on Street Fighter EX, Tetris 99, Fighting EX Layer and more, has sadly passed away due to heart failure

As announced in a statement by Arika president Akira Nishitani (and translated by Time Extension, thank you), Akira Kurabayashi, a director at the combined dev/publishing studio and a creator whose work spans three decades and several genres, sadly passed away as a result of heart failure late last week.

Kurabayashi initially worked as a programmer on smaller titles at Taito, including early 2.5D fighting game Fighters' Impact (later localised as VS. in America). He then moved to Arika in 1996 and continued his work in 2.5D fighters with the Street Fighter EX series, a subseries which took the originator of the fighting game genre into the third dimension for the first time. While that subseries didn't last long, its spiritual successor Fighting EX Layer made waves in 2018, bringing back original characters from SFEX and even including Fatal Fury's Terry Bogard.

Fighting EX Layer started out as an April Fools' joke back in 2017, but the reaction to the trailer from fans who missed the SFEX series convinced Arika to bring the series back, even without the Capcom IP. The final result is an interesting 2.5D fighter that combines conventional mechanics, such as magic series combos and supers, with the unique (for better and worse) Gougi system, where of in-match perks are chosen from a deck of cards at roundstart. I had a good time playing it for its systems (and Terry is very fun in it), but the Gougi system brought to mind Street Fighter x Tekken's infamous paid Gem debacle, which no one should be reminded of. Anyway. In addition to 2.5D fighters, Kurabayashi also contributed to Tetris: The Grandmaster, Tetris 99, PAC-MAN 99, and ARIKA's collaboration with SNK in the form of their 'SNK Revamp Project'.

Nishitani gave a few personal words towards Kurabayashi in the statement:

"We are deeply saddened to have lost a dear colleague who has created numerous works with us and supported Arika for many years. We express our heartfelt respect and gratitude for his immense achievements to date, and we will cherish and carry on the skills, experience, and attitude toward game development that he left behind. I would like to express my deepest gratitude for the kindness you showed us during their lifetime, and I respectfully pray for the repose of their soul."

Freddie Gibbs' apocalypse bunker is what will unlock Hurricanes for the first time in GTA 6

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 hurricanes are a weather phenomenon that only unlock through the questline about Freddie's Bunker - specifically, Freddie Gibbs, acclaimed rapper, who has built a prepper apocalypse bunker that he wants you to test the security measures for. This ultimately leads to a choice about whether you want to stay in Freddie's bunker or leave when the Hurricane comes down on you, which I'll also explain the consequences of below.

To unlock Hurricanes as a weather condition you need to do the following:

From that point on, Hurricanes will be a random sporadic weather occurrence. They don't change a huge amount about the game, with the exception that long-distance visibility is lower, and that roads are more slippery when driving. They might also impact any attempt to control flying vehicles (I've yet to test that).

To start this questline, you need to go to the unnamed compound on the west side of North Leonard County, near the north of the map. It's actually pretty hard to miss: this is a big facility ringed by electric fences, marked by a sign called "Ripe Pickins Grove", and when you get close, an automated system will blare at you, telling you to leave.

There's no given reason for you to ignore this, except, y'know, video game logic. If somebody is telling you not to be somewhere, that's a place worth investigating.

To get inside, head to the North section of the compound to see a water tower near the perimeter. You can climb up the tower, then jump down from the walkway over the compound fence to get inside.

Once you're in, you need to go to the Bunker at the South side. Be warned though: there are lots of landmines that explode when you get too close. Thankfully they do very little damage, but you can spot them by using Focus mode if you want to be certain.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

You'll also get attacked by drones. These have low health, which is good, but they're small and fairly agile, making them hard to hit. Take time to aim your shots and use focus to hit the propellers to bring them down.

Once you reach the bunker, interact with the door to speak to the occupant over the intercom. Though annoyed his defenses failed, he also sees the value in having somebody test them for weaknesses. He tells you he'll text you later when he's upgraded them further so you can try again.

For me, that text took 4-7 in-game days, roughly speaking, though it's possible it's tied to something else like mission progression instead of in-game time. Either way, just go and play more GTA 6, and you'll get the message eventually.

On your second invitation, the water tower ladder has been blocked off, stopping you from getting past the fence that way. What you want to do instead is go to the Northwest corner of the compound, where you'll find a tractor and a section of fence that's collapsed at the top. If you drive the tractor to the fence and raise the scoop, you can climb up it and leap over the electric wires to get inside.

From here, I highly recommend you grab the excavator ahead of you. It's borderline undestroyable and you can simply roll over the mines and have drones bounce off you until you reach the Bunker again.

Once you reach it, you'll meet the occupants, including the owner Freddie Gibbs. He's built an apocalypse prepper bunker, but his guests are quickly growing bored and abandon him. He'll give you the tour though, which is when he gets a hurricane warning and the choice about what to do comes up.

When Freddie sees the Hurricane, he gives you the chance to either stay in his bunker or leave. There are actually some mildly significant consequences to this choice:

Of these two, I'd say it's better to stay. As much as a hit to your GTA 6 relationship status can be a blow, you can always rebuild it with a little patience and care, and the unique car is valuable enough to make it worth it (it also counts as one of Randy's desired cars, as he's after the Benefactor Dubsta that Freddie's is a custom variant of).

After this point, no matter your choice, Hurricanes will occur randomly throughout your time spent playing GTA 6. As mentioned above, they're rare and largely cosmetic impacts on the world, but are still an interesting change to the landscape.

#3833. Star Wars: Galactic Racer studio "didn't dream" Biddy Blas would be as popular as he is

"He's always known exactly who he is, and he wears it proudly."

Fuse Games, the developer of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, has said it "didn't dream" the pod racing game's background character Biddy Blas would become as popular as he has.

Since Galactic Racer's release in October, Blas - who resembles a short, humanoid crocodile (officially a crocin) - has become a viral sensation. The combination of his unexpected swagger and ridiculous high-pitched Huttese monologues - performed irresistibly by actor Richard Summers-Calvert - have made him a fan favourite, especially his catchphrase "scrib doon" (which means "write it down").

"Here's a name for you, amateur!" Blas tells the player upon meeting them, albeit in Huttese. "Biddy Blas. Write it down. Tattoo it on your arm, and someday your arm will be worth millions!"

Fuse Games shared a comment from Biddy Blas creator and Galactic Racer narrative designer Ren Alex-Rose about the character's success. "We always suspected Biddy Blas would be a popular member of the Galactic League, but we didn't dream of just how popular he'd become," Alex-Rose said.

"He was an incredibly enjoyable character to build, from our early ideation of a small, angry non-human character (who we lovingly referred to as our cast's 'chaos goblin') to recording his sometimes-absurdist dialogue with Blas' voice actor, who took the crocin to a whole new level.

"It's been great watching Biddy Blas emerge into his assured self, as well as seeing the community embrace him for it. He's always known exactly who he is, and he wears it proudly."

Blas' breakout success was praised by Lucasfilm producer Craig Derrick, who said his social feeds were filled with posts about Galactic Racer, though mostly about Biddy Blas. And the enthusiasm actor Richard Summers-Calvert was greeted with during October's MCM Comic-Con in London, which I attended, was palpable. There's a nice video of him doing Blas' voice on Instagram.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer was awarded a full five stars in Eurogamer's review. "Both a surprisingly fun Roguelite campaign and a racing treat for Criterion fans, this is just wonderful stuff," wrote Christian Donlan.

#3832. Vote now for 2026's RPS 100: Reader Edition

For the past six years, the team at RPS have got together to pick what we consider to be the best 100 games you can play on PC. There's very little science involved, and we try not to get too hung up on what games should make the cut. From year to year, our rankings and choices vary wildly as the formation and tastes of the team changes.

However, our definitive list isn't always met with a chorus of approval and cheers of 'Hear, hear!', "'Well done!', and 'Couldn't have said it better myself!', so we also have the RPS 100: Reader Edition. This is your chance to submit your ten favourite PC games of all time. Your votes will be tallied up with all the other submissions from our other readers and we will produce a list of the community's top 100.

We've just finished revealing what we currently consider to be the Best PC games of all time and now it's your turn.

Using this very Google Form you can submit up to ten votes for your favourite PC games of all time. I will then tally them up with all the other votes from RPS's readers and produce a list of the community's top 100.

Now, a note on scoring. The game you put in 10th place will be awarded one point, 9th place will be worth two, 8th place will be worth three, and so on until you reach your top pick, which will be worth ten points. Please write the full game name (and include the year of release if there are multiple titles in a series with the same name, such as Doom (1993) and Doom (2016)). If in doubt, check how the game is titled on Steam.

Last year, I implemented a change to create a greater variety of games on the list. I combined series scores, so if one reader voted for Civilization IV and another voted for Civilization VI, the scores of both were combined and the entry would be for the Civilization series. I also shared the breakdown of the votes for each title in the entry, so you could see which was most popular within the series.

I will be doing the same again this year, as we saw a lot more games that wouldn't have made the cut otherwise. However, I will try to do a better job of separating out games that are very different from one another even if they are in the same series. Warcraft 3 and World of Warcraft are both Warcraft games, but, admittedly, they aren't similar games. I would ask for some leeway on this, though, as not every example is clear cut. Should Alpha Centauri be counted among the Civilization games? Are Final Fantasy XIV and Final Fantasy Tactics - The Ivalice Chronicles truly worlds away from the other games in the Final Fantasy series?

This does also mean that one-shot games can struggle to compete against games which are part of longrunning series. After all, Crimson Skies isn't just competing against Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020), it is competing against votes for any and all Microsoft Flight Simulator games ever released. Unfortunately, this is a cost of the system, but I prefer the variety that comes from seeing more games represented instead of several separate entries for games within the same series.

We also invite you to tell us why you've chosen each game. This is entirely voluntary, you can simply enter the game titles if you would prefer. However, I'll choose a selection of what readers have said about winning games so we can better understand why the RPS community loves these games. Try not to write any more than 100 words. If you have more to say you can always drop it in the comments of the list when we publish it at the end of the year.

To cast your votes, please make sure you complete this form by 5pm GMT on Sunday, December 6th.

Rockstar recreated an embarrassing mishap in Florida infrastructure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When you're exploring a world as realistic and well-observed as GTA 6's Leonida, it's rare for a piece of benign infrastructure to stick out. But on night one of my playthrough, I clocked some weird streetlights.

A stylistic choice by Rockstar? Maybe, but it's awfully specific, and I had a feeling there was a deeper intention behind it. So I DMed my buddy Henry, an honest-to-god Floridian who was also playing GTA 6, and asked what's up. At first he thought strange streetlights in the Key Lento area of the map were special lights meant to not disorient turtles, but those are typically red, so probably not. And that doesn't explain the purple ones.

So Henry reached out to friends in south Florida, the region that Leonida's biggest cities are based on, and they cracked the case wide open.

"The purple [lights] are definitely real. We have a ton of them down here because whoever is in charge of that in the government bought a bunch of defective lights," the anonymous Floridian responded.

Yes, actual Florida cities are lit by these dubiously dim, yet undeniably cool purple lamps. According to ClickOrlando, residents first started reporting the purple streetlights in 2023. They put up hundreds of these things across the state before they started malfunctioning—it was such a kerfuffle that the government eventually released a statement saying their vendor really screwed the pooch.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Apparently the cause was a "spectral shift caused by phosphor displacement," which essentially means the LED lights were always blue, but the coating that was supposed to make appear yellow or white or whatever didn't work. The powers that be said the malfunctioning lights would be replaced, but judging by our own sources in the state, they haven't gotten them all.

So that's fun. If you already heard about this somewhere (other than your Floridian friend), it's probably because YouTuber AnyAustin also clocked these lights in his video published yesterday. Glad I'm not the only one who couldn't resist this rabbit hole.

I like how Rockstar didn't go overboard with these lights—just like the genuine article, they're in and around parts of Leonida, but not everywhere. I'm still not sure how to explain the turquoise ones, though. A lot of local news, Reddit, and YouTube skimming did not produce a clear answer, other than other cities in America that do have green streetlights sometimes. Perhaps Key Lento has lamps busted in a slightly different way, or it's just a calming shade of blue that Rockstar thought looked nice. It does, to be fair.

#3830. Nvidia's latest graphics card driver appears to be unnecessarily writing to PC SSDs, something that's dumb, annoying and definitely warrants reverting

Ooh, an Nvidia-related story that isn't about their now former CEO allegedly getting amorous with someone. I wonder what it's abou-oh. Oh no. It looks like Nvidia's latest GeForce driver, 621.24, is needlessly writing vast amounts of data to PC SSDs.

As noted by PC Gamer, reports of driver 621.24 writing more than it should to SSDs have popped up across various forums and Reddit.

Some instances of the bug, which doesn't appear to be affecting everyone, have the driver writing up to 30GB every hour. For context, it'd take a bugged driver writing that much thousands of hours to break a gaming SSD with a typical endurance rating in the hundreds of terabytes. However, that doesn't mean this is anything less than a pretty bad bug. As such, reverting to the previous driver, 621.01, is a good idea if you're on 621.24 and suspect it of writing chunks of gigabytes to your SSD.

In order to check if that's going on, open task manager, head to the 'details' tab, right click on the column header, click 'select columns', select 'I/O write bytes' from the menu of check boxes that brings up, then look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe'. The number next that exe is in bytes, so you'll need to do a bit of maths to work out if it's writing mere MB or globs of GB.

Bizarrely, the affected 621.24 driver still hasn't been pulled by Nvidia as of writing, meaning it can still be downloaded by people who might not be aware of any issues and think 'ooh, haven't checked I'm on the latest driver in a while.' The driver was released on November 12th, so it's not a brand new arrival that the company just haven't had a chance to look into yet.

Here's hoping that it is fixed or replaced ASAP, if it hasn't been by the time you read this. AMD look to have dealt with a similar issue recently, and I'd like to think driver updates across all cards aren't going to be some form of permanent Russian roulette going forwards.

#3829. Poll: What Review Score Would You Give GTA 6?

It's been a full week since GTA 6 released, if you can believe it. After years and years and years of waiting for it to finally arrive, I hope that you've been enjoying your life in Leonida.

I say that because it's quite obviously time to rate the game for yourself.

To recap, GTA 6 remains the highest rated title ever released. It now has over 160 reviews on Metacritic and it still sits at a frankly staggering 99 score. It's extremely difficult to imagine that it'll ever be equalled — never mind beaten.

But it hasn't all been smooth sailing for Rockstar's latest. The game's been review bombed for a variety of reasons by frustrated users — once again sparking conversations surrounding the legitimacy of user reviews in general.

Counter to that, it's worth noting that GTA 6 is exceptionally highly rated on the PS Store, where people actually have to buy the game before giving it a score out of five. 389,000 ratings and it's at 4.78 — which equates to 92% of players giving it a full five stars.

You don't have to agree with all the praise, though — that's what these polls are for. Maybe you like GTA 6 but still think that it's overrated, or perhaps it's struggling to live up to your lofty expectations.

Our view is simple enough: Push Square editor Sammy dubbed it "the greatest open world game ever made" in his GTA 6 PS5 review, awarding the title a very rare 10/10.

"Rockstar has set a new sandbox standard here, with a world that feels alive and populated with real people; Leonida is a place where it appears almost anything can happen at any time," he wrote — and I don't think he's wrong!

Review GTA 6 (PS5) - The Greatest Open World Game Ever Made

Guide GTA 6 Guide: All Guides & Collectibles

@GeeEssEff Scales are typically meant to have hypothetical extremes. It's not usually expected that anything will ever touch extremities. Let's say, for example, that you give a game a 10, even though it's flawed. What happens when an even better and more polished game releases? What score does the remaster of the 10/10 game GTAVI earn then?

It can't be a 10.5 or an 11. How are you going to quantify or indicate the improvements, which, say, smooth out the frame rate or improve environmental detail? With a 10? But now, the game with the poorer frame rate is apparently the same quality as the one with the superior frame rate.

Therefore, a 10 is meant to be a hypothetically attainable score, similar to, say, approaching infinity in mathematics, or 100% in statistics, or the two extremes of the political compass.

Not everyone is going to agree. Everyone has their own system. But if someone suggests as much (that 10/10 should be unequivocally perfect), this is probably the logical which applies.

#3828. GTA 6 players are already pulling off high-flying tricks and other impressive stunts, just days after launch

One of the best things to emerge from Grand Theft Auto over the years has been the community's truly spectacular stunts: players soaring under bridges, leaping across buildings, and more. And with GTA 6's release this week, we've seen the first signs of the trend continuing in a brand-new world.

This TikTok video by user Gstitz from early in GTA 6, for instance, claims to be the "world's first" demonstration of a Mallard flying sideways between a narrow gap in a large building. It takes several attempts, but they eventually pull off the stunt without crashing or broken parts.

Another video from Hazardous is a more grounded (literally) look at Grand Theft Auto 6, and shows the YouTuber flinging motorbikes and cars around the map as they explore promising high-risk jumps. Some of these locations are tied to in-game challenges, so there are certainly breadcrumbs placed by Rockstar to encourage such ventures.

Granted, these are far from the truly absurd stunts we've seen in prior Grand Theft Auto games. But as a firing gun for the wider community, it's a great start. They're also among the most impressive things we've seen in GTA 6's opening week.

It's doubtless been an eventful few days though. Players have been entranced by the slapstick violence and in-game social media. Even UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the game, despite not having time to actually play it. Eurogamer editor-in-chief Chris Tapsell also came away impressed, lauding it in his five star GTA 6 review.

If you're playing the game and need some help, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough, and our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheat list.

Team Cherry has confirmed that Hollow Knight: Silksong's Sea of Sorrow DLC will be releasing on December 11, 2026.

This was confirmed in the developer's "Cherry Time! Special Presentation," which featured a new trailer for the expansion alongside the announcement of its release date (and the showcase of three lovely looking indie titles). And thankfully we're not going to be waiting very long, as Sea of Sorrow is coming out in two weeks, with the devs hyping it up as an "expansion unlike any we've done before."

As promised, Sea of Sorrow is a "high-seas adventure," with the trailer featuring Hornet arriving on a boat to uncharted shores and taking the fight to pirate bugs who yelp "arghhh" when you beat them with a very Donkey Kong Country 2-coded sound effect. We also saw her blasting out of cannons, climbing net ladders, and getting in scraps with multiple giant pirate bosses.

We knew its release had to be soon as the DLC, which was announced shortly after Silksong launched, was previously given a 2026 release window – although given the reveal to release timeline of the game itself, it's perhaps no surprise that some have not been so trusting, especially when that date vanished on the game's physical copy.

While Silksong famously started out as a DLC for the original Hollow Knight, it's easy to forget that the original got multiple DLC packs, with four free expansions released within its two years. Team Cherry didn't confirm what DLC is still to come for Silksong, but given it's the "first big content update" I'm sure fans will be fed for a while yet.

Katana Zero pulls a Hollow Knight: Silksong - the beloved action game's DLC is now "the size of a full sequel" after 7 years of development.

#3826. 13 arrested in Shanghai as police crackdown on bootleg Final Fantasy 7 Tifa figurine operation

Chinese police have arrested 13 individuals in Shanghai allegedly involved in a bootleg Final Fantasy 7 Tifa figurine business, after consumers reported the operation. They are currently being investigated on suspicion of selling infringing reproductions.

Reported by Gamespark, the police cracked down on the operation which involved the seizure of around $300,000 of goods related to the figurines.

The investigation started in May, after police received reports from concerned members of the public about the Tifa figurines. They were made from different materials than official figurines, and after confirming the illegitimacy of these products with the rights holders, Square Enix, police determined these businesses were not authorised to be producing such goods and went to work.

The appearance of these counterfeits were deemed identical to the real merch, and therefore the alleged crime was deemed infringement of official goods. These counterfeits also came in different sizes, some of which were more expensive than the originals and customisabile.

Looking at pictures taken by local outlet Shangguan News (and put side-by-side by Automaton), you can see the official Tifa figurine (right) next to the counterfeit version (left). Both show Tifa in a blue dress, though the materials used are clearly different.

The Muv-Luv trilogy is a visual novel phenomenon that's tough to explain. The first game's a schlocky high school romance generally considered a chore to get through before the good stuff, when the protagonist of that story finds himself out of his depth as a mecha pilot fighting aliens in an apocalyptic warzone. It becomes a dense, twisty, and increasingly serious saga that just happens to star a dropkick hero right out of a harem anime.

Muv-Luv's popular enough to have a bunch of spin-offs, the latest being a gacha game called Muv-Luv Girls Garden in which you collect girls to pilot mecha in automated battles, and of course said girls are romanceable. This caused a problem, as players discovered when they made it to some of the adult scenes only to find dialogue in which characters repeated at each other, "I can't provide a translation for explicit sexual content."

Yeah, Muv-Luv Girls Garden was translated into English with AI. The Steam page does mention this in its AI-generated content disclosure, though hilariously it does so in untranslated Japanese: "1部ローカライズに生成AIを使用しています。"

Players are unimpressed, with the Steam user rating dropping to Mostly Negative. As one user review puts it, "What if you want to goon But God says I'm unable to provide a translation for this text because it contains explicit sexual content."

Other user reviews complain about changes to the original artwork, with characters having accessories like teddy bears and hair ribbons taken away, as well as being given larger breasts or made to look taller. It's tougher to emphasize with players who are mad that characters in an adult game have been changed to look less like 12-year-olds, especially given the pressure put on Valve by payment processors to remove certain kinds of games from Steam.
